# Justia U.S. 8th Circuit Court of Appeals Opinion Summaries
Posted in: Labor & Employment Law

**Alvarenga v. Blanche**

Maria Lily Alvarenga and her son, E.D.B.A., are Honduran nationals who entered the United States unlawfully in April 2019. After encountering Border Patrol, Alvarenga was placed in removal proceedings for being present without admission or parole. She admitted to being a Honduran citizen and lacking a visa or passport.
In the second phase of proceedings, Alvarenga sought relief from removal, claiming asylum, statutory withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture (CAT), based on alleged gang-related persecution by MS-13. She stated MS-13 attempted to recruit her son, threatened him, and threatened to harm her, though no physical harm occurred, and the threats were not acted upon. Alvarenga did not report these incidents to Honduran authorities.
An Immigration Judge determined Alvarenga was removable and denied her claims for relief, finding insufficient evidence of persecution based on a protected ground and no demonstration of government acquiescence in torture. Alvarenga appealed to the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA), asserting that the IJ erred and violated her due process rights by committing procedural mistakes. The BIA dismissed the appeal, affirming the IJ’s decision.The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reviewed Alvarenga’s petition.
The court held that Alvarenga’s due process claim failed because she did not demonstrate prejudice from any alleged procedural errors. Regarding asylum and withholding of removal, the court found substantial evidence supported the BIA’s determination that Alvarenga’s proposed social group was not sufficiently particular or socially distinct, and her claim based on imputed political opinion was not substantiated by precedent. For CAT relief, the court concluded Alvarenga failed to show government acquiescence or awareness of the alleged threats.

Attorney General Todd Blanche (Getty Images)

Attorney General Todd Blanche (Getty Images)

Attorney General Todd Blanche on Tuesday ordered Justice Department civil litigators to help defend immigration detention cases, saying detainees have filed more than 97,000 habeas petitions since January 2025.
The three-page memo, addressed to all department employees, draws on attorneys from the antitrust, civil, civil rights, and environmental divisions, as well as the U.S. Trustee Program — a pool Blanche estimated at about 2,000 litigators.

Attorneys in his own office and in the offices of the deputy and associate attorneys general will also take cases.
U.S. attorneys' offices, which have carried the load, will stay in the fight. Blanche wrote that many "have been overwhelmed by the influx of petitions and impracticable procedures set by the courts."

A habeas corpus petition asks a federal judge to decide whether a person is being held lawfully. Blanche said about 10,000 new petitions have come in since October alone.
In a post on X announcing the move, he went further, describing "frivolous habeas petitions used by corrupt judges to release criminal aliens."

The memo directs the head of the Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys to coordinate with the prosecutors' offices facing the most petitions and orders senior officials to recommend an aggressive appeals strategy within 30 days.

The Eighth Circuit has denied a petition for review from a Honduran mother and her son whose applications for asylum, withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture were denied by an Immigration Judge and affirmed by the Board. The petitioners argued that procedural errors by the Immigration Judge violated due process. The court assumed there were errors without deciding the question, but held that the petitioners failed to show prejudice, since the mother conceded Honduran citizenship and offered only speculation about evidence she might have presented.

The court also rejected the proposed particular social group of "Honduran citizens who refused to comply with gang demands" for lack of particularity and social distinction and held that generalized opposition to gang activity does not establish an imputed political opinion under INS v. # Maria Alvarenga v. Todd Blanche
October 8, 2026 · Federal Court Ruling
Record confidence: Unresolved
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit on October 8, 2026, denied a petition for review by Maria Lily Alvarenga and her son, Honduran nationals who entered the United States unlawfully in 2019, leaving in place the Board of Immigration Appeals' order that they be removed to Honduras. Writing for a panel of Chief Judge Colloton and Judges Erickson and Grasz, Judge Grasz held that Alvarenga showed no prejudice from the immigration judge's alleged procedural errors; that her asylum and withholding claims, based on MS-13's attempts to recruit her son, did not rest on a qualifying protected ground; and that substantial evidence supported denying protection under the Convention Against Torture because generalized claims that criminal organizations had infiltrated the Honduran police and judiciary did not show government acquiescence. The case is No. 25-2780.

November 10, 2026
A lawful permanent resident from Guatemala became concerned about her niece, who was living with her father. Upon checking her father’s phone, she discovered nude photos and videos of her niece. Rather than contacting law enforcement, she took pictures and videos of these pornographic images with her own phone and sent them to her niece’s mother in Guatemala. After her father was arrested for sex crimes, the niece moved in with her. Months later, the niece reported to police that the resident used the images as leverage and to protect her father. Police found the images on the resident’s phone, leading to her conviction for child exploitation under Indiana law.The Department of Homeland Security charged her as removable for committing an aggravated felony (sexual abuse of a minor) and a crime of child abuse under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). An Immigration Judge ordered her removal. She appealed to the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA), which dismissed her appeal and later denied her motion for reconsideration. She then petitioned for review of both orders.The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reviewed the case de novo. The court held that the Indiana statute under which she was convicted fits within the broad federal definition of “crime of child abuse” for purposes of removal under the INA. The court also found that she did not demonstrate a realistic probability that Indiana would apply its statute to conduct outside the generic federal definition. Additionally, the court upheld the BIA’s determination that she committed a “particularly serious crime,” barring her from withholding of removal and protection under the Convention Against Torture. To qualify, you generally must show that you are a **refugee**. Under U.S. law, a refugee is someone who was persecuted, or has a **well-founded fear** of being persecuted in the future, because of at least one of five protected grounds:

## United States Court of Appeals, Eighth Circuit.
###
Maria Lily ALVARENGA; E.D.B.A., Petitioners v. Todd BLANCHE, Attorney General of the United States, Respondent
### No. 25-2780
### Decided: October 08, 2026

Maria Lily Alvarenga and her son, E.D.B.A., petition for review of the Board of Immigration Appeals' (BIA) order affirming an immigration judge's (IJ) decision ordering them removed to Honduras and denying their claims for asylum, statutory withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture (CAT). We deny the petition.
I. Background
Alvarenga 1 and E.D.B.A. are Honduran nationals who unlawfully entered the United States in April 2019. After Border Patrol officers encountered Alvarenga, the Department of Homeland Security placed her into removal proceedings for being present without admission or parole. Removal proceedings are divided into two phases: the first determines an alien's removability; the second determines whether an alien qualifies for relief from removal. At the first hearing, the IJ determined Alvarenga was removable after Alvarenga admitted she was a citizen of Honduras and lacked a visa or passport when she arrived at the United States border.

Because Alvarenga did not sufficiently prove the persecution was because of a protected ground nor demonstrate government acquiescence in the face of torture, the IJ denied Alvarenga's claims for relief. Alvarenga appealed to the BIA, challenging the IJ's denial of relief from removal and claiming her due process rights were violated because the IJ committed procedural errors. The BIA dismissed the appeal, and Alvarenga now petitions this court for review.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit on October 8, 2026, denied a petition for review by Maria Lily Alvarenga and her son, Honduran nationals who entered the United States unlawfully in 2019, leaving in place the Board of Immigration Appeals' order that they be removed to Honduras. webiq.snippet:
Maria Lily Alvarenga and her son, E.D.B.A., are Honduran nationals who entered the United States unlawfully in April 2019. 

Alvarenga sought asylum, statutory withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture based on MS-13’s attempts to recruit her son. After he refused, gang members threatened to kidnap him and to “do something” to Alvarenga. Her son stopped attending school to avoid the gang, but MS-13 never physically harmed Alvarenga or carried out the kidnapping threats. Alvarenga did not report the gang’s conduct to law enforcement. The immigration judge denied relief, and the Board of Immigration Appeals dismissed her appeal.

The Eighth Circuit denied the petition for review. Assuming without deciding that procedural errors occurred during the removal proceedings, the court held that Alvarenga failed to establish prejudice. She identified no plausible basis for concluding that she was lawfully present or entitled to admission and did not explain what evidence she could have presented had the immigration judge asked additional questions.

The court also upheld the denial of asylum and withholding of removal. Alvarenga’s proposed social group—Honduran citizens who refused to comply with gang demands—was not sufficiently particular or socially distinct, and generalized resistance to gang recruitment did not establish persecution based on an actual or imputed political opinion. Because she failed to satisfy the asylum standard, she necessarily failed to meet the more demanding standard for withholding of removal.

Substantial evidence also supported denial of CAT protection. Alvarenga never reported the gang’s conduct to Honduran police and therefore did not show that officials had prior awareness of a threat of torture. Her generalized assertions that criminal organizations had infiltrated Honduras’s police and judiciary did not establish that public officials would acquiesce or remain willfully blind to her torture.

They sought asylum, statutory withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture, claiming MS-13 threatened them after the son refused gang recruitment. The court reviewed the due process claim de novo and found no prejudice because the petitioners admitted they lacked a visa or passport and offered no evidence they could have been lawfully admitted.
